nutshell: Multi-object tracking (MOT) datasets like MOT15/16/17/20 show a pronounced long-tail distribution in pedestrian trajectory lengths - a few identities ('head classes') appear in thousands of frames while most ('tail classes') appear in only a handful. This paper is the first to identify that problem specifically for MOT and proposes two viewpoint-specific data augmentation strategies (SVA for static cameras, DVA using diffusion for moving cameras) plus a Group Softmax module that partitions pedestrian identities by sample count so the Re-ID branch's softmax loss doesn't let head classes suppress tail classes.
contributions: First identification and analysis of pedestrian trajectory long-tail distribution as a problem specific to multi-object tracking data (rather than just importing generic long-tail-recognition fixes wholesale).

Stationary Camera View Data Augmentation (SVA): uses SAM to segment tail-class pedestrians and synthetically extends their trajectories via 'backtracking continuation' (reversed re-pasting of the existing track after it ends) and 'prediction continuation' (Kalman-filter-predicted positions pasted before the track begins).

Dynamic Camera View Data Augmentation (DVA): for moving-camera footage, segments pedestrians out (SAM), inpaints the background (Navier-Stokes), re-stylizes it via Stable Diffusion, and merges the pedestrians back in - with a per-epoch stochastic original-vs-augmented image selection (Eq. 4) to avoid overfitting to diffusion artifacts.

Group Softmax (GS): partitions the M pedestrian identity classes into K groups by training-sample count and computes softmax + cross-entropy independently per group instead of globally, preventing head-class weights from dominating tail-class weights in the Re-ID branch's loss.

Plugs into two existing SOTA joint-detection-and-tracking trackers (FairMOT, CSTrack) with consistent gains across MOT15/16/17/20, including a data-efficiency result where FairMOT+their method trained only on MOT20 outperforms baseline FairMOT trained on a much larger mixed multi-dataset corpus (Table 4).
deficiencies: On MOT17 - one of the two most heavily used, best-annotated benchmarks - the method actually loses ground on some key metrics: FairMOT+Ours drops IDF1 by 0.1 and MOTA by 0.3 versus baseline, and identity switches rise from 4,329 to 4,776 (about +10%), which the text discussion glosses over by focusing only on the small HOTA gain (+0.2).

The paper's headline gains cluster almost entirely on MOT15 and MOT20 - the oldest (pre-standardized-annotation) and the smallest/most narrowly-scoped (dense-crowd-only) benchmarks respectively - while gains on the more mainstream MOT16/17 benchmarks are marginal (0.1-0.5 HOTA). This leaves open whether the method is really addressing long-tail distribution specifically, or exploiting weaker/noisier baselines on lower-quality or narrower data that's easier to improve on.

The ablation (Table 5) shows each of the three components contributing under 1 point individually on MOT17 val (SVA +0.5 MOTA/+0.5 IDF1, DVA on top +0.2/+0.2, GS on top +0.3/+0.4), and all results throughout the paper - including the long-tail-method comparison in Table 1 and the threshold sweep in Table 6 - are single runs with no repeated trials or variance reporting, which is thin support for three separately-motivated architectural additions.

The DVA image-selection-threshold sweep (Table 6) bounces non-monotonically across values of Ts (e.g. 0.7 -> 69.0/72.5, 0.8 -> 69.0/70.6, 0.9 -> 69.3/73.4, 1.0 -> 68.3/71.0) with no visible trend; picking Ts=0.9 as 'best' from a single noisy run per setting reads more like selecting the best point in noise than demonstrating a real optimum.
notable: The DVA pipeline explicitly flags the well-known risk that training on diffusion-augmented data can overweight spurious generative artifacts (citing Antoniou et al. 2017 and He et al. 2022), and addresses it with a simple per-image, per-epoch stochastic choice between the real and diffusion-augmented version (Eq. 4) rather than always training on the augmented data - a lightweight, reusable pattern for anyone else using diffusion-based augmentation. Also worth flagging for a person-ReID literature review specifically: this is a general multi-object-tracking paper (built on FairMOT/CSTrack, evaluated on MOTChallenge benchmarks) where Re-ID is only one sub-module (the appearance-embedding branch of a joint detection-and-tracking system), not the paper's central task.
